result:
Picture a very smart friend locked in a room with no phone and no window. The room has a slot in the door.

Your friend knows a lot, but only what's already in their head. They can't see today's booking calendar or open a machine manual.

On the door you tape a **menu of services**, for example "check the calendar for a date" and "look up a page in the manual". Each item has a short description of what it does and what details you need to give. This menu is the tool list.

A student asks, "Is the laser cutter free Thursday?" You slide the question through the slot. Your friend can't check, but they can read the menu. They write a note back: *"Please run 'check the calendar' for Thursday, laser cutter."* That note is the **tool call**.

Your friend did not look anything up. You are standing outside the door. You read the note, walk to the calendar, read it, and slide the result back: *"Booked 2–4pm, free otherwise."* Your friend then writes the answer for the student.

So the model never runs anything. It only writes a request in a set format, and your program does the real work and passes the result back. This is the loop you already know.

**Where the analogy breaks:** your friend remembers the whole conversation. A model doesn't, so your program re-sends the full history with every note. That is why many back-and-forths cost more, which matters for your budget.

Quick check: in your makerspace assistant, who actually books the machine, the model or your program? What does the model contribute?

If you'd like, I can turn this into a short lesson on writing good menu descriptions for your tools.
